diagonal.example: The visitors' undoing was caused by a diagonal ball from the right which was nodded into the six-yard area by Ian Evatt and finished off by Campbell.
diagonal.exampleSense: Having a slanted or oblique direction.

straight.o: From Middle English streight, streght, streiȝt, the past participle of strecchen (“to stretch”), from Old English streċċan (past participle ġestreaht, ġestreht), from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan (“to stretch”). Cognate with Scots straicht (“straight”), Dutch gestrekt (“stretched”), German gestreckt (“stretched”), Danish strakt (“stretched”), Faroese and Norn strekti (“stretched”), Icelandic strekkti (“stretched”), Norwegian strekte (“stretched”), Swedish sträckte (“stretched”). Doublet of straught. Equivalent to stretch + -ed. In some senses, conflated with strait (“narrow, constricted”), which is from Latin strictus via Old French estreit.
straight.example: After four straight wins, Mudchester United are top of the league.
straight.exampleSense: In a row, in unbroken sequence; consecutive.

circle.o: From Middle English circle, cercle, from Old French cercle and Latin circulus, diminutive of Latin circus (“circle, circus”), from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos, “circle, ring”), related to Old English hring (“ring”). Compare also Old English ċircul (“circle, zodiac”), which came from the same Latin source. By surface analysis, Latin circ(us) + -(u)le.
circle.example: The crank moves in a circle.
circle.exampleSense: Any shape, curve or arrangement of objects that approximates to or resembles the geometric figures. A curve that more or less forms part or all of a circle.

round.o:
adj: From Middle English round, rounde, from Old Northern French roünt, rund, Old French ront, runt, reont ( > French rond), from both Late Latin retundus and the original Latin rotundus. The noun developed partly from the adjective and partly from the corresponding French noun rond. Doublet of rotund.

verb: From Middle English rounen, from Old English rūnian (“to whisper, talk low, talk secrets, consipre, talk secretly”), from Proto-Germanic *rūnōną (“to talk secrets, whisper, decide”), *raunijaną (“to investigate, examine, prove”), from Proto-Indo-European *(e)rewə-, *(e)rwō- (“to trace, find out, look out”). Cognate with Scots roun (“to converse with in whispers, speak privately”), Middle Low German rūnen (“to whisper”), Middle Dutch ruinen (“to whisper”), German raunen (“to whisper, murmur”), Old English rūn (“whisper, secret, mystery”), Swedish röna (“to meet with, experience”). More at rune.
round.example: Daniel underwent one round of chemotherapy in February but stopped after that single treatment, citing religious beliefs.
round.exampleSense: A single individual portion or dose of medicine.

dot.o: From Middle English *dot, dotte, from Old English dott (“a dot, point”), from Proto-West Germanic *dott, from Proto-Germanic *duttaz (“wisp”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Dot, Dotte (“a clump”), Dutch dot (“lump, knot, clod”), Low German Dutte (“a plug”), dialectal Swedish dott (“a little heap, bunch, clump”).
dot.example: The alphabetical signals are made up of combinations of dots and of lines of different lengths.
dot.exampleSense: One of the two symbols used in Morse code.

sphere.o: From Middle English spere, from Old French sphere, from Late Latin sphēra, earlier Latin sphaera (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”), of unknown origin. Not related to superficially similar Persian سپهر (sepehr, “sky”) . Displaced Old English cliewen, þoþor, and æppel.
sphere.example: So your orientation changes a little bit but it sinks in that the world is a sphere, and you're going around it, sometimes under it, sideways, or over it.
sphere.exampleSense: An object which appears to be bounded by a sphere; a round object, a ball.

cone.o: From Middle English cone (“corner, angle”) and conoun (“cone”), from Medieval Latin cōnus, cōnon (“cone, wedge, peak”), from Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos, “cone, spinning top, pine cone”). Reinforced by Middle French cone, from the same Graeco-Latin source.
cone.example: Under the old method the material coned at the bottom of the borehole and as a result it would not go under houses and buildings.

extent.o: From Middle English extente, from Anglo-Norman extente and Old French estente (“valuation of land, stretch of land”), from estendre, extendre (“extend”) (or from Latin extentus), from Latin extendere (See extend.)
extent.example: The extent of his knowledge of the language is a few scattered words.
extent.exampleSense: The space, area, volume, etc., to which something extends.

width.o: PIE word *dwóh₁ From wide + -th (abstract nominal suffix), possibly by analogy with Old Norse vídd (“width”), though this is unlikely, as the word is not attested before the end of the 16th century and was historically unknown in Scots and the traditional dialect of Northern England, where one would expect Old Norse influence to be the strongest (these varieties traditionally employed wideness instead). Replaced Middle English wide, wyde (“width”).
width.example: Manchester United like to play with width.
width.exampleSense: The use of all the width of the pitch, from one side to the other.

length.o: From Middle English lengthe, from Old English lengþ, lengþu, from Proto-West Germanic *langiþu, from Proto-Germanic *langiþō, equivalent to long + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Scots lenth, lainth (“length”), Saterland Frisian Loangte (“length”), West Frisian lingte, langte (“length”), Dutch lengte (“length”), German Low German Längde, Längd, Längte, Längt (“length”), Danish længde (“length”), Swedish längd (“length”), Icelandic lengd (“length”).
length.example: Happiness makes up in height for what it lacks in length.

decimal.o: Borrowed from Late Latin, Medieval Latin decimalis, from Latin decimus, from decem (“ten”) + adjective suffix -alis.
decimal.example: What is ⁷⁄₂₃ as a decimal?
decimal.exampleSense: A number expressed in the base-ten system, (particularly) a fractional numeral written in this system.

percent.o: From New Latin per centum (“by the hundred”).
percent.example: Twelve percent of the world’s population now relies directly or indirectly on the fisheries industry.
percent.exampleSense: For every hundred (used with preceding numeral to form a noun phrase expressing a proportion).

per cent.example: London Transport fares are now about 92 per cent. above prewar, but it is claimed that costs have risen by 140 per cent.

proportion.o: From Middle English proporcion, from Old French proportion, from Latin prōportiō (“comparative relation, proportion, symmetry, analogy”), from pro (“for, before”) + portio (“share, part”); see portion. By surface analysis, pro- + portion.
proportion.example: The image of Christ made in Pilate's time after his own proportion.
proportion.exampleSense: The relation of one part to another or to the whole with respect to magnitude, quantity, or degree.

rate.o:
noun: From Middle English rate, from Old French rate, from Medieval Latin rata, from Latin prō ratā parte (“according to a fixed part”), from ratus (“fixed”), from rērī (“think, deem, judge, estimate", originally "reckon, calculate”).

verb: From Middle English raten (“to scold, chide”), from Old Norse hrata (“to refuse, reject, slight, find fault with”), from Proto-Germanic *hratōną (“to sway, shake”), from Proto-Indo-European *krad- (“to swing”). Cognate with Swedish rata (“to reject, refuse, find fault, slight”), Norwegian rata (“to reject, cast aside”), Old English hratian (“to rush, hasten”).

verb: Related to, or a variant of, ret. (Found dialectally also as rait.)
rate.example: At the height of his powers, he was producing pictures at the rate of four a year.
rate.exampleSense: The proportional relationship between one amount, value etc. and another.

ratio.o: Borrowed from Latin ratiō. Doublet of ration and reason.
ratio.example: It is essential that you ratio anyone who comes for your honour.
ratio.exampleSense: To respond to a post or message on social media in a greater number than the number of likes the post receives, especially to condemn or mock the original poster.

fraction.o: From Middle English fraccioun (“a breaking”), from Anglo-Norman, Old French fraccion, from Medieval Latin fractio (“a fragment, portion”), from earlier Latin fractio (“a breaking, a breaking into pieces”), from fractus, past participle of frangere (“to break”) (whence English frangible), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (English break). Doublet of frazione.
fraction.example: After kick-off was delayed because of crowd congestion, Torquay went closest to scoring in a cagey opening 30 minutes, when Danny Stevens saw a fierce shot from the edge of the area swerve a fraction wide.

scale.o:
noun: From Middle English scale, from Latin scāla, usually in plural scālae (“a flight of steps, stairs, staircase, ladder”), for *skand-slā, from scandō (“to climb”); see scan, ascend, descend, etc. Doublet of scala.

noun: From Middle English scale, from Old French escale, from Frankish and/or Old High German skala, from Proto-Germanic *skalō. Cognate with Old English sċealu (“shell, husk”), whence the modern doublet shale. Further cognate with Dutch schaal, German Schale, French écale.

noun: Inherited from Northern Middle English scale (non-Northern scole), from Old Norse skál (“bowl”) from Proto-Germanic *skēlō. Compare Danish skål (“bowl, cup”), Dutch schaal, German Schale, Old High German scāla, Old English scealu (“cup”).
scale.example: The magnitude of an earthquake is measured on the open-ended Richter scale.
scale.exampleSense: An ordered, usually numerical sequence used for measurement; means of assigning a magnitude.

ounce.o:
noun: From Middle English ounce, unce, from Middle French once, from Latin uncia (“Roman ounce, various similar units”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one”). Doublet of a, one, inch, uncia, onça, onza, oka, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

noun: From Middle French once, from Old French lonce (“lynx”), by false division (the l was thought to be the article), from Italian lonza, ultimately from Ancient Greek λύγξ (lúnx, “lynx”). Doublet of onza and lynx.
ounce.example: He didn't feel even an ounce of regret for his actions.
ounce.exampleSense: Any small amount, a little bit.

density.o: Borrowed from Middle French densité or Latin densitas. Morphologically dense + -ity.
density.example: In the past two years, NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope has located nearly 3,000 exoplanet candidates ranging from sub-Earth-sized minions to gas giants that dwarf our own Jupiter. Their densities range from that of styrofoam to iron.
density.exampleSense: A measure of the mass of matter contained by a unit volume.

Fahrenheit.o: From German Fahrenheit, named after Prussian scientist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit.
Fahrenheit.example: For example, in the Fahrenheit scale 212°F is the boiling point of water.
Fahrenheit.exampleSense: Describing a temperature scale originally defined as having 0°F as the lowest temperature obtainable with a mixture of ice and salt, and 96°F as the temperature of the human body, and now defined with 32°F equal to 0°C, and each degree Fahrenheit equal to 5/9 of a degree Celsius or 5/9 kelvin.

mercury.o: The noun is derived from Middle English mercurie (“metallic chemical element, quicksilver; a plant, probably goosefoot (genus Chenopodium); (possibly) dog’s mercury (Mercurialis perennis); etc.”), borrowed from Late Latin mercurius (“metallic chemical element, quicksilver”), Latin Mercurius (“Mercury, the Roman god of commerce, communication, etc.; the planet Mercury; etc.”), possibly from merc-, a stem of merx (“goods, wares; merchandise”); further etymology uncertain, possibly: * from Etruscan; or * from Proto-Indo-European *merǵ- (“to divide”), or *merkʷ- (“to grasp; to take”). The suffix -urius is also thought to be from Etruscan. Noun sense 1 (“metallic chemical element”) is from the association in medieval alchemy of the seven known metals—gold, silver, quicksilver, copper, iron, tin, and lead—with the Sun, the Moon, and the planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. An analogy was probably also drawn between the element being liquid at room temperature, and the Roman god Mercury’s attribute of swiftness. Noun sense 2 (“senses relating to plants”) is derived from mercurial (“(obsolete) any of the plants now known as mercury”, noun), from Middle English mercurial (“a plant, probably goosefoot (genus Chenopodium); (possibly) dog’s mercury (Mercurialis perennis)”, noun) from Anglo-Norman mercurial, Old French mercurial, or directly from their etymon Latin mercuriālis (“a plant, probably annual mercury (Mercurialis annua)”), short for herba mercuriālis (“(probably) annual mercury”, literally “herb or plant of the god Mercury”). Mercuriālis (“pertaining to the Roman god Mercury”, adjective) is derived from Mercurius (“the Roman god Mercury”) (see above) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship from nouns). Noun sense 2.2.2.1 (“Blitum bonus-henricus”) is from the fact that this plant was often confused with annual mercury (noun sense 2.1). The verb is derived from the noun.
mercury.example: The mercury there has averaged 37.6°C, 2.3°C above the February norm.
mercury.exampleSense: Ambient pressure or temperature (from the use of mercury in barometers and thermometers).

battery.o: Borrowed from Middle French batterie, from Old French baterie (“action of beating”), from batre (“beat”), from Latin battuō (“beat”), from Gaulish. Doublet of batterie. By surface analysis, batter + -y. The electrical sense was coined by American polymath Benjamin Franklin by analogy with a military battery that his series of Leyden jars resembled.
battery.example: Schoolchildren take a battery of standard tests to measure their progress.

volt.o:
noun: Named after Italian physicist Alessandro Volta. For the surname, see Italian Volta.

noun: From French volte.
volt.example: If the volt, ampere and ohm were taken as the absolute units, the practical units would be the ampere, begohm and begavolt, names just as convenient as ampere, coulomb and farad.
volt.exampleSense: In the International System of Units, the derived unit of electrical potential and electromotive force (voltage); the potential difference across a conductor when a current of one ampere uses one watt of power. Symbol: V

radiate.o:
verb: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus, perfect passive participle of radiō (“to radiate, furnish with spokes, give out rays, radiate, shine”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from radius (“a spoke, ray”).

adj: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

noun: From a substantivation of the above adjective through the associated taxon's name (Radiata), see -ate (noun-forming suffix).
radiate.example: Oban is not a terminus; its routes radiate by sea, rail and road.
radiate.exampleSense: To extend, send or spread out from a center like radii.

emit.example: The controls then emit client-side HTML code that is appended to the final page output.
emit.exampleSense: To send out or give off.

transparent.o:
adj: Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārēns, trānspārēntis (“transparent”), present participle of transpareō, from Latin trans + pareō. Displaced native Old English þurhsīene.

noun: From trans- (“transgender or transsexual”) + parent.
transparent.example: The waters of the lake were transparent until the factory dumped waste there.
transparent.exampleSense: See-through, clear; having the property that light passes through it almost undisturbed, such that one can see through it clearly.

hollow.o:
noun: From Middle English holow, holowe, holwe, holwȝ, holgh, from Old English holh (“a hollow”), from Proto-West Germanic *holh, from Proto-Germanic *hulhwą, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *ḱólḱwos. Cognate with Old High German huliwa and hulwa, Middle High German hülwe. Related to hole.

adj: From Middle English holowe, holwe, holuȝ, holgh, from the noun (see above).

verb: Compare holler.
hollow.example: He built himself a cabin in a hollow high up in the Rockies.

ozone.o: From German Ozon, coined 1840 by Christian Friedrich Schönbein, from Ancient Greek ὄζον (ózon), neuter participle of ὄζω (ózō, “I smell”), in reference to its pungent odour. The “fresh air” sense is from an erroneous former belief that seaweed contains and releases ozone.
ozone.example: Lightning flashed again, the thunder came a second later. It rained harder. The smell of ozone was strong. You could feel the charge in the air.
ozone.exampleSense: An allotrope of oxygen (symbol O₃) having three atoms in the molecule instead of the usual two; it is a toxic gas, generated from oxygen by electrical discharge.

gravity.o: Borrowed from French gravité (“seriousness, solemnity; severity; (physics) gravity”), or from its etymon Latin gravitās (“heaviness, weight; seriousness; severity”), equivalent to grave (“serious”) + -ity (suffix forming nouns, especially abstract nouns). Gravitās is derived from gravis (“heavy; grave, serious”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷreh₂- (“heavy”)) + -tās (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns indicating states of being). The English word was first used figuratively, and gained the senses relating to physical qualities in the 17th century. Doublet of gravitas.
gravity.example: Do you know that gravity is pulling at you, tugging at you, trying to drag you down, from the moment you awake in the morning till you tumble into bed at night?
gravity.exampleSense: The phenomenon that, on earth, objects have weight; the similar phenomenon on other celestial bodies such as the moon.

friction.o: From Middle French friction and directly from Latin frictionem, nom. frictio (“a rubbing, rubbing down”).
friction.example: The frictions should at first be very gentle, and performed with a view to restore heat, and not to force the blood towards the heart, which in drowned persons is already too much distended with it.
friction.exampleSense: Massage of the body to restore circulation.

eccentric.o: From Middle French excentrique, from Medieval Latin eccentricus, from Ancient Greek ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros, “not having the earth as the center of an orbit”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + κέντρον (kéntron, “point”). Equivalent to ex- + -centric.
eccentric.example: Oospores may be centric, subcentric, subeccentric or eccentric. Antheridial branches may or may not be present, and are androgynous, monoclinous, diclinous or hypogynous.
eccentric.exampleSense: Having or being an oospore with a single large oil globule on one side that displaces much of the ooplasm and forces the ooplasts to one side.

displace.example: Freud considered shyness to be evidence of displaced narcissism.

boil.o:
noun: From Middle English bile, büle (“boil, tumor”), from Old English bȳl, bȳle (“boil, swelling”), from Proto-Germanic *būlijō, *būlō (“boil”). Akin to Dutch buil (“boil, swelling”), German Beule (“boil, hump”), Icelandic beyla (“swelling, hump”). The expected form is bile; the rounding of the diphthong could be caused by the initial b- and/or by association with etymology 2.

noun: From Middle English boillen, from Old French boillir (see French bouillir) from Latin bullīre (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (“bubble”). Displaced native Old English weallan (intransitive) and wiellan (transitive). More at wall, well.
boil.example: Add the noodles when the water comes to the boil.
boil.exampleSense: The point at which fluid begins to change to a vapour; the boiling point.

melt.o: From Middle English melten, from a merger of Old English meltan (intransitive) and mieltan (transitive), both meaning “to melt, digest,” from Proto-West Germanic *meltan and *maltijan, from Proto-Germanic *meltaną and *maltijaną, both from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meld- (“melt”). Cognate with Icelandic melta (“to digest”).
melt.example: When the weather is warm, the snowman will disappear; he will melt.
melt.exampleSense: To change (or to be changed) from a solid state to a liquid state, usually by a gradual heat.

dissolve.o: Recorded since c. 1374 (displacing Old English toliesan) as Middle English dissolven, from Latin dissolvere (“to loosen up, break apart”) but with the sense from Anglo-Norman dissoldre (variant of Old French dissoudre), itself from dis- (“apart”) + solvere (“to loose, loosen”). By surface analysis, dis- + solve.
dissolve.example: For one people to dissolve the political bands which have connected them with another.
dissolve.exampleSense: To break the continuity of; to disconnect; to loosen; to undo; to separate.

rust.o:
noun: From Middle English rust, rost, roust, from Old English rust, rūst (“rust”), from Proto-West Germanic *rust, from Proto-Germanic *rustaz (“rust”), from Proto-Indo-European *rudʰso- (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”). Cognate with Scots roust (“rust”), Saterland Frisian rust (“rust”), West Frisian roast (“rust”), Dutch roest (“rust”), German Rost (“rust”), Danish rust (“rust”), Swedish rost (“rust”), Norwegian rust, ryst (“rust”), Finnish ruoste, Estonian rooste. Related to red.

verb: From Middle English rusten, from the noun (see above).
rust.example: The rust on my bicycle chain made cycling to work very dangerous.
rust.exampleSense: The deteriorated state of iron or steel as a result of moisture and oxidation.

ferment.o: From Middle English ferment, from Middle French ferment, from Latin fermentāre (“to leaven, ferment”), from fermentum (“substance causing fermentation”), possibly from contraction of *fervimentum, from fervēre. See also fervent.
ferment.example: Ye vigorous swains! while youth ferments your blood.
ferment.exampleSense: To stir up, agitate, cause unrest or excitement in.

dilute.o: From Latin dīlūtus, from dīluere (“to wash away, dissolve, cause to melt, dilute”), from dī-, dis- (“away, apart”) + luere (“to wash”). See lave, and compare deluge.
dilute.example: Clean the panel with a dilute, neutral cleaner.

acid.o: From French acide, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”), from aceō (“to be sour”). Doublet of agita.
acid.example: In the end, though, there is one sure way to distinguish a real hippie from his assorted sympathizers: hippies drop acid. That is, real hippies frequently, if irregularly, ingest LSD.

noxious.o: From Latin noxius (“hurtful, injurious”), from noxa (“hurt, injury”), from nocere (“to hurt, injure”); see nocent.
noxious.example: [...] many old sewers have been neglected and are in dire need of repair. If that repair does not come in time, the result is noxious and potentially hazardous.

static.o: Modern Latin staticus, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós), from ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to make stand”). By surface analysis, stasis + -tic.
static.example: Damaged Hologram: --alled Reapers. [static]... the Citadel... [static] ...overwhelmed... [static] ...only hope... [static]...
static.exampleSense: Interference on a broadcast signal caused by atmospheric disturbances; heard as crackles on radio, or seen as random specks on television.

inert.o: From French inerte, from Latin iners (“inactive, inert”).

inherent.o: From Latin inhaerentem, accusative singular of inhaerēns, present active participle of inhaereō (“to be closely connected with; to adhere to”).
inherent.example: There is a stern melancholy in his dark features, inherent and engrossing, which rivets the attention.
inherent.exampleSense: Naturally as part or consequence of something.

formula.o: Learned borrowing from Latin fōrmula (“a small pattern or mold, form, rule, principle, method, formula”), diminutive of forma (“a form”). See form.
formula.example: x=(-b±√)/(2a) is a formula for finding the roots of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0.

component.o: Borrowed from Latin compōnēns, compōnēntis, present participle of compōnō (“assemble, put together”).
component.example: A CPU is a component of a computer.
component.exampleSense: A smaller, self-contained part of a larger entity. Often refers to a manufactured object that is part of a larger device.

compose.o: From Middle English composen, from Old French composer (“to compose, compound, adjust, settle”), from com- + poser, as an adaptation of Latin componere (“to put together, compose”), from com- (“together”) + ponere (“to put, place”).
compose.example: The editor composed a historical journal from many individual letters.
compose.exampleSense: To make something by merging parts.

mixture.o: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French misture, from Latin mixtūra (“a mixing”), from mixtus, perfect passive participle of misceō (“mix”); compare mix.
mixture.example: The mixture of sulphuric acid and water produces heat.

blend.o: From Middle English blenden, either from Old English blandan, blondan, ġeblandan, ġeblendan or from Old Norse blanda (“to blend, mix”) (which was originally a strong verb with the present-tense stem blend; compare blendingr (“a blending, a mixture; a half-breed”)), whence also Danish blande, or from a blend of the Old English and Old Norse terms; both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *blandaną (“to blend; mix; combine”). Compare Middle Dutch blanden (“to mix”), Gothic 𐌱𐌻𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌰𐌽 (blandan), Old Church Slavonic блєсти (blesti, “to go astray”).
blend.example: To make hummus you need to blend chickpeas, olive oil, lemon juice and garlic.
blend.exampleSense: To mingle; to mix; to unite intimately; to pass or shade insensibly into each other.

theory.o: Borrowed from Middle French théorie, a learned borrowing from Late Latin theōria, borrowed from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).
theory.example: In its most proper acceptation, theory means the completed result of philosophical induction from experience.
theory.exampleSense: A coherent statement or set of ideas that explains observed facts or phenomena and correctly predicts new facts or phenomena not previously observed, or which sets out the laws and principles of something known or observed; a hypothesis confirmed by observation, experiment etc.

empirical.example: The lengths were calculated according to the empirical rules of the trade.
empirical.exampleSense: Pertaining to or based on experience (often, in contrast with having a basis in theoretical explanation).

practical.o: From Middle English practical, practicale, praktycall, from Medieval Latin practicālis.
practical.example: All in all, Jack's a very practical chap.
practical.exampleSense: Of a person, having skills or knowledge that are practical.

doctrine.o: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin doctrina (“teaching, instruction, learning, knowledge”), from doctor (“a teacher”), from docere (“to teach”); see doctor.
doctrine.example: What is the understanding of marriage and family in orthodox Marxist doctrine?
doctrine.exampleSense: The body of teachings of an ideology, most often a religion, or of an ideological or religious leader, organization, group, or text.

principle.o: From Middle English principle, from Old French principe, from Latin prīncipium (“beginning, foundation”), from prīnceps (“first”). By surface analysis, prīmus (“first”) + -ceps (“catcher”); the former ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”); see also prince.
principle.example: The Pauli Exclusion Principle prevents two fermions from occupying the same state.
principle.exampleSense: A rule or law of nature, or the basic idea on how the laws of nature are applied.

discipline.o: From Middle English [Term?], from Anglo-Norman, from Old French descipline, from Latin disciplina (“instruction”), from discipulus (“pupil”), influenced by disco (“to learn”), from Proto-Indo-European *dek- (“(cause to) accept”).
discipline.example: Economics is a messy discipline: too fluid to be a science, too rigorous to be an art.
discipline.exampleSense: A specific branch of knowledge, learning, or practice.

term.o:
noun: From Middle English terme, borrowed from Old French terme, from Latin terminus (“a bound, boundary, limit, end; in Medieval Latin, also a time, period, word, covenant, etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *térmn̥ (“stump, end, boundary”). Doublet of terminus and termon. Old English had termen, from the same source.

noun: Clipping of terminal.

verb: Short for terminate, termination, terminated employee, etc.
term.example: The subject and predicate of a proposition are, after Aristotle, together called its terms or extremes.
term.exampleSense: The subject or the predicate of a proposition; one of the three component parts of a syllogism, each one of which is used twice.

semester.o: From German Semester, from New Latin sēmestris (“lasting six months”), from sex (“six”) + mēnsis (“month”).
semester.example: I will graduate at the end of the spring semester.
semester.exampleSense: Half of a school year (US) or academic year such as autumn or spring semester.

timetable.example: The timetable has been changed several times since it was first announced.
timetable.exampleSense: A tabular schedule of events with the times at which they occur, especially times of arrivals and departures.

schedule.o: Inherited from Middle English cedule, from Middle French cedule (whence French cédule), from Old French cedule, from Late Latin schedula (“papyrus strip”), diminutive of Latin scheda, from Ancient Greek σχέδη (skhédē, “papyrus leaf”), from Proto-Hellenic *skʰíďďō, from Proto-Indo-European *skid-yé-ti, from *skeyd- (“to divide, split”). Doublet of cedula and cedule. This word was historically pronounced /ˈsɛdjuːl/, /ˈsɛdʒuːl/; the pronunciations with /ʃ/ and /sk/ are due to the spelling (the latter may have been reinforced by learned influence); compare schism.
schedule.example: To complete on time, we must follow the schedule.
schedule.exampleSense: A procedural plan, usually but not necessarily tabular in nature, indicating a sequence of operations and the planned times at which those operations are to occur.

deadline.o: According to the Oxford English Dictionary, early usage refers to lines that do not move, such as one used in angling. Slightly later American usage refers to a boundary in a prison which prisoners must not cross. There is only indirect evidence that the sense of "due date" may be connected with this use of the term in prison camps during the American Civil War, when it referred to a physical line or boundary beyond which prisoners were shot. In 1904, in a report from the US Department of Commerce and Labor, the term is used for "minimum work goals" (and in contrast to bonus line): for example, as a typographer the line could be 18,000 ems per day; should one not cross this line, then that could have negative consequences. In 1917, the term is attested as a printing term for a guideline on the bed of a printing press beyond which text will not print. Three years later, the term is found in print in the sense of "time limit" in the closely connected publishing industry, indicating the time after which material would not make it into a newspaper or periodical.
deadline.example: I must make this deadline or my boss will kill me!
deadline.exampleSense: A time limit in the form of a date on or before which something must be completed.

course.o: From Middle English cours, from Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (“run”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”). Doublet of cursus and cour.
course.example: I need to take a French course.
course.exampleSense: A sequence of events. A learning programme a series of lectures or lessons in a particular subject

lesson.o: From Middle English lessoun, from Old French leçon, from Latin lēctiō, lēctiōnem (“a reading”), from legō (“to read; to gather”). Doublet of lection.
lesson.example: She would give her a lesson for walking so late.
lesson.exampleSense: A severe lecture; reproof; rebuke; warning.

curriculum.o: Borrowed from Latin curriculum (“course”), derived from currō (“run, move quickly”). Doublet of curricle.
curriculum.example: Drawing on texts recommended in curricula and controlling for two countries with benchmarked curricula improves the external representativeness of the corpus.
curriculum.exampleSense: The set of standards schools are required to teach all students.

seminar.o: From German Seminar, from Latin sēminārium, from sēmen (“seed”). Compare seminary.

forum.o: From Latin forum (“public market place, forum”). Doublet of fuero and door.
forum.example: Trish was an admin on three forums, and had no trouble at all when it came to moderating them.
forum.exampleSense: An Internet message board where users can post messages regarding one or more topics of discussion.

syllabus.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin syllabus (“list”), which arose from accusative plural syllabōs appearing as a corruption of sittybās (accusative plural of sittyba, from Ancient Greek σιττύβα (sittúba, “parchment label; table of contents”)) in a 1470s edition of Cicero's “Ad Atticum” IV.5 and 8, influenced by the stem of Ancient Greek συλλαμβάνω (sullambánō, “to put together”).
syllabus.example: In the first half of the year, teachers attended the training workshop for the new K-10 Chinese syllabus. In July, almost all the teachers attended the teacher training courses provided by OCAC.
syllabus.exampleSense: A summary of topics which will be covered during an academic course, or a text or lecture.

system.o: Partly borrowed from Middle French sisteme, systeme, partly directly from its etymon Late Latin systēma (“harmony; musical scale; set of celestial objects; set of troops; system”), from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “musical scale; organized body; whole made of several parts or members”), from σῠνίστημῐ (sŭnístēmĭ, “to combine, organize”) + -μᾰ (-mă, resultative suffix). σῠνίστημῐ is from σῠν- (sŭn-, “with, together”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand (up)”). Cognate with Dutch systeem, modern French système, German System, Italian sistema, Portuguese sistema, Spanish sistema. Doublet of systema.
system.example: There are eight planets in the solar system.
system.exampleSense: A group or set of related things that operate together as a complex whole. A system in which two or more objects are bound to each other by gravity.

rudimentary.example: His grasp of rudimentary English allowed him at least to do the shopping.
rudimentary.exampleSense: Basic; minimal; with less than, or only the minimum, necessary.

basic.example: Rice is a basic for many Asian villagers.
basic.exampleSense: A necessary commodity, a staple requirement.

fundamental.o: From Late Latin fundamentālis, from Latin fundamentum (“foundation”), from fundō (“to lay the foundation (of something), to found”), from fundus (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn.
fundamental.example: Personal leadership is a fundamental of successful government.
fundamental.exampleSense: A collection of essential component ideas that are often grouped together to serve as the foundational basis of a complex idea.

elementary.o: From Middle English elementare, from Latin elementārius (“elementary”), from elementum (“one of the four elements of antiquity; fundamentals”) + -ārius (adjective-forming suffix). Cognate with French élémentaire. By surface analysis, element + -ary.
elementary.example: At Lakeside Elementary I learned to appreciate the forest.

profound.o: From Middle English profound, profounde, from Anglo-Norman profound, from Old French profont, profonde, from Latin profundus (“deep, profound”), from prō + fundus (“bottom; foundation”).
profound.example: Of the profound corruption of this class there can be no doubt.
profound.exampleSense: Characterized by intensity; deeply felt; pervading

surface.o: Borrowed from Middle French surface. By surface analysis, sur- + face. Doublet of superficies.
surface.example: Use the lowest light level required. Be mindful of surface conditions, as some surfaces may reflect more light into the night sky than was intended.
surface.exampleSense: The overside or up-side of a flat object such as a table, or of a liquid.

compulsory.o: Borrowed from Late Latin compulsorius, from Latin compulsus. Displaced native Old English ġenīedelīċ.

prerequisite.example: A degree is a prerequisite for entry into this profession.
prerequisite.exampleSense: Something that is required as necessary or indispensable, or as a prior condition of something else.

selective.example: The selective algorithm excludes the redundant classifiers to construct a streamlined ensemble learning.
selective.exampleSense: Of or relating to the process of selection.

elective.example: I still need to decide which electives to take along with my compulsory courses next semester.
elective.exampleSense: Something that is an option or may be freely chosen, especially a course of study.

assignment.o: From Middle English assignement, from Old French assignement. By surface analysis, assign + -ment.
assignment.example: The assignment of the lease has not been finalised yet.
assignment.exampleSense: A transfer of a right or benefit from one person to another.

submit.o: From Middle English submitten, borrowed from Latin submittere, infinitive of submittō (“place under, yield”), from sub (“under, from below, up”) + mitto (“to send”). Compare upsend.
submit.example: They will not submit to the destruction of their rights.
submit.exampleSense: To yield or give way to another.

preview.o: From pre- + view; compare Old French preveü, past participle of preveoir (“to foresee”).

review.o: From Middle English revewe, reveue, from Old French reveüe, revue (Modern French: revue), feminine form of reveü, past participle of reveoir (French: revoir), from Latin revideō, from re- +videō (“see, observe”) (English: video). Equivalent to re- + view. Compare retrospect. Doublet of revue.
review.example: The newspaper review was full of praise for the play.
review.exampleSense: An account intended as a critical evaluation of a text or a piece of work.

revise.o: Borrowed from Middle French réviser, from Latin revīsō, from re- + vīsō (“examine”), frequentative of videō (“see”).
revise.example: I've only just begun to revise for my exams.
revise.exampleSense: To look over again (something previously written or learned), especially in preparation for an examination.

inspect.o: From Latin inspectum, past participle of inspicere (“to look into”), from in (“in”) + specere (“to look at”), equivalent to in- + -spect.
inspect.exampleSense: To examine critically or carefully; especially, to search out problems or determine condition; to scrutinize.

consult.o: From Middle French consulter, from Latin cōnsultum, from cōnsultus, from cōnsulō.
consult.example: Let us consult upon to-morrow's business.
consult.exampleSense: To seek the opinion or advice of another; to take counsel; to deliberate together; to confer; to advise.

skim.o: From Middle English skemen, skymen, variants of scumen, from Old French escumer (“to remove scum”), from escume (“froth, foam”), from Frankish *skūm (“froth, foam”), from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz (“foam”), from Proto-Indo-European *skew- (“to cover, conceal”). See scum.
skim.example: They skim over a science in a very night superficial survey.
skim.exampleSense: To hasten along with superficial attention.

scan.o: From late Middle English scanne (“to mark off verse to show metrical structure”), from earlier scanden, from Late Latin scandere (“to scan verse”), from Classical Latin scandō (“to climb, rise, mount”), from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to jump, dart, climb, scale, scan”).
scan.example: She scanned the passage carefully but could not find what she was looking for.
scan.exampleSense: To examine sequentially, carefully, or critically; to scrutinize; to behold closely.

scrutinise.example: But few MPs could claim to have followed and scrutinised Government transport policy to the extent that she has over the past decade.
scrutinise.exampleSense: To examine something with great care.

scrutinize.example: Those pronounced him youngest who scrutinized his face the closest.
scrutinize.exampleSense: To examine something with great care or detail, as to look for hidden or obscure flaws.

recite.o:
verb: From Middle English reciten, from Old French reciter, from Latin recitō.

verb: From re- + cite.
recite.example: Janice is able to recite pi to 100 decimals.
recite.exampleSense: To repeat aloud (some passage, poem or other text previously memorized, or in front of one's eyes), often before an audience.

dictate.o:
noun: First attested in 1581; borrowed from Latin dictātum (“a thing said, something dictated”), substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of dictātus, the perfect passive participle of dictō (“pronounce or declare repeatedly; dictate”), frequentative of dīcō (“say, speak”). Doublet of diktat.

verb: First attested in 1577; borrowed from Latin dictātus, perfect passive participle of dictō (“to pronounce or declare repeatedly; to dictate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), frequentative of dīcō (“say, speak”).
dictate.example: The French teacher dictated a passage from Victor Hugo.
dictate.exampleSense: To speak in order for someone to write down the words.

examination.o: From Middle English examinacioun, from Old French examinacion, from Latin exāminātiō. Morphologically examine + -ation.
examination.example: The question of the plausibility of the counter-factual is seen as key in all three discussions of allohistorical fiction (as it is in Demandt's and Ferguson's examinations of allohistory) (cf. Rodiek 25–26; Ritter 15–16; Helbig 32).

exam.example: Thin sections were stained with lead citrate and then examed using 1200EX electron microscope (JEOL, Tokyo, Japan).

test.o:
noun: From Middle English test, teste, from Old French test, teste (“an earthen vessel, especially a pot in which metals were tried”), from Latin testum (“the lid of an earthen vessel, an earthen vessel, an earthen pot”), from *terstus, past participle of the root *tersa (“dry land”). See terra, thirst. The examination sense came via metaphor of the metallurgical sense: the way a metallurgist puts to the test his gold, a teacher may put to the test her students' knowledge. Displaced Old English afandung.

noun: From Middle English teste, from Old French teste, test and Latin testis (“one who attests, a witness”).
test.example: Climbing the mountain tested our stamina.
test.exampleSense: To challenge, to put a strain on (something).

quiz.o: Attested since the 1780s, of unknown origin. * The Century Dictionary suggests it was originally applied to a popular toy, from a dialectal variant of whiz. * The Random House Dictionary suggests the original sense was "odd person" (circa 1780). * Others suggest the meaning "hoax" was original (1796), shifting to the meaning "interrogate" (1847) under the influence of question and inquisitive. * Some say without evidence it was invented by a late-18th-century Dublin theatre proprietor who bet he could add a new nonsense word to the English language; he had the word painted on walls all over the city, and the morning after, everyone was talking about it (The Pre-Victorian Drama in Dublin). * Others suggest it was originally quies (1847), Latin qui es? (who are you?), traditionally the first question in oral Latin exams. They suggest that it was first used as a noun from 1867, and the spelling quiz first recorded in 1886, but this is demonstrably incorrect. * A further derivation, assuming that the original sense is "good, ingenuous, harmless man, overly conventional, pedantic, rule-bound man, square; nerd; oddball, eccentric", is based on a column from 1785 which claims that the origin is a jocular translation of the Horace quotation vir bonus est quis as "the good man is a quiz" at Cambridge.
quiz.example: We came second in the pub quiz.
quiz.exampleSense: A competition in the answering of questions.

presentation.o: From Old French presentation (French présentation), from Latin praesentātiōnem, accusative singular of praesentātiō (“representation, exhibition”). Morphologically present + -ation.
presentation.example: Prayers are sometimes a presentation of mere desires.
presentation.exampleSense: The act of presenting, or something presented.

plagiarise.o: From plagiary + -ise, ultimately from Latin plagiare (“to kidnap, to abduct”).

plagiarize.o: From plagiary + -ize, ultimately from Latin plagiare (“to kidnap, to abduct”).

copy.o:
noun: From Middle English copy, copie, from Old French copie (“abundance, plenty; transcript, copy”), from Medieval Latin copia (“reproduction, transcript”), from Latin cōpia (“plenty, abundance”), from *coopia, from co- (“together”) + ops (“wealth, riches”). More at opulent.

verb: From Middle English copien, from Old French copier and Medieval Latin cōpiō.
copy.example: I have not the vanity to think my copy equal to the original.
copy.exampleSense: The result of copying; an identical or nearly identical duplicate of an original.

print.o: From Middle English *printen, prenten, preenten, an apheretic form of emprinten, enprinten (“to impress; imprint”) (see imprint). Compare Dutch prenten (“to imprint”), Middle Low German prenten (“to print; write”), Danish prente (“to print”), Swedish prenta (“to write German letters”). Compare also Late Old French printer, preindre (“to press”), from Latin premere (“to press”).
print.example: From the moment he prints, he must expect to hear no more truth.
print.exampleSense: To publish in a book, newspaper, etc.

thesis.o: From Late Middle English thesis (“lowering of the voice”) and also borrowed directly from its etymon Latin thesis (“proposition, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from Ancient Greek θέσῐς (thésĭs, “arrangement, placement, setting; conclusion, position, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from τῐ́θημῐ (tĭ́thēmĭ, “to place, put, set; to put down in writing; to consider as, regard”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do; to place, put”)) + -σῐς (-sĭs, suffix forming abstract nouns or nouns of action, process, or result). The English word is a doublet of deed. Sense 1.1 (“proposition or statement supported by arguments”) is adopted from antithesis. Sense 1.4 (“initial stage of reasoning”) was first used by the German philosopher Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814), and later applied to the dialectical method of his countryman, the philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770–1831). The plural form theses is borrowed from Latin thesēs, from Ancient Greek θέσεις (théseis).

essay.o:
noun: Since late 16th century, borrowed from Middle French essay, essai (“essay”), meaning coined by Montaigne at the same time, from the same words with the earlier meanings 'experiment; assay; attempt', from Old French essay, essai, assay, assai, from Latin exagium (“weight; weighing, testing on the balance”), from exigere + -ium.

verb: From Middle French essayer, essaier, from Old French essaiier, essayer, essaier, assaiier, assayer, assaier, from essay, essai, assay, assai (“attempt; assay; experiment”) as above.
essay.example: He retraced his steps to the front gate, which he essayed to open.

paper.o: From Middle English paper, from Anglo-Norman paper, from Old Catalan paper, borrowed from Latin papȳrus (and given the Catalan suffix -er), from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros).
paper.example: Draw on the paper! Not on the walls!
paper.exampleSense: A sheet material typically used for writing on or printing on (or as a non-waterproof container), usually made by draining cellulose fibres from a suspension in water.

project.o: From Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth, extend; expel”). Compare typologically Russian прики́дывать (prikídyvatʹ), прики́дка (prikídka) (akin to кида́ть (kidátʹ)); набро́сок (nabrósok) (akin to броса́ть (brosátʹ)).
project.example: The proposal with China would involve a project to create artificial rain.
project.exampleSense: A planned endeavor, usually with a specific goal and accomplished in several steps or stages.

outset.o:
noun: From out- + set, replacing earlier outsetting.

verb: From out- + set.
outset.example: He agreed and understood from the outset, so don't bother explaining again.
outset.exampleSense: Onset; the beginning or initial stage of something.

outline.example: From this point of vantage, we were able to gain an impression of the massive outlines of the main structure, and its intricate maze of girders.
outline.exampleSense: The outer shape of an object or figure.

point.o:
noun: From Middle English poynt, from Old French point m (“dot; minute amount”), from Latin pūnctum (“a hole punched in; a point, puncture”), substantive use of pūnctus m, perfect passive participle of pungō (“to prick, punch”); alternatively, from Old French pointe f (“sharp tip”), from Latin pūncta f (past participle), all from Proto-Italic *pungō (“to sting, prick”). Mostly displaced native Middle English ord (“point”), from Old English ord (“point”). Doublet of pointe, ponto, puncto, punctum, punt, and punto.

verb: From Middle English pointen, poynten, from Old French pointier, pointer, poynter, from point from Latin pūnctum.

verb: From Middle English pointen, poynten, by apheresis of apointen, appointen, appoynten. See appoint.
point.example: We should meet at a pre-arranged point.
point.exampleSense: A small discrete division or individual feature of something. A specific location or place, seen as a spatial position.

gist.o:
noun: The noun is derived from Old French gist, a noun use of the third person singular indicative of gesir (“to lie down”) (modern French gésir; compare Anglo-Norman (cest) action gist (literally “(law) (this) action lies”)), from Latin iacēre, the present active infinitive of iaceō (“to lie down, lie prostrate, recline”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)yeh₁- (“to throw”) (probably in the sense of something being thrown down). The verb is derived from the noun. The programming sense is a genericized trademark of GitHub Gist, introduced 2008.

noun: From Middle English giste, geste (“resting or stopping place, hostel, lodgings; food, refreshment; (figurative) seat of the soul”), from Old French giste (“resting place”) (modern French gîte (“lodging, shelter; self-catering holiday home”)), a noun use of the past participle form of gesir (“to lie down”): see etymology
gist.example: I don't wanna belabor my point; I'm sure you get the gist.
gist.exampleSense: The main idea or substance, or the most essential part, of a longer or more complicated matter; the crux, the heart, the pith.

opinion.o: From English opine + -ion, from Middle English opinion, opinioun, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French opinion, from Latin opīniō, from opīnor (“to opine”). Displaced native Old English wēna.
opinion.example: I would like to know your opinions on the new filing system.
opinion.exampleSense: A belief, judgment or perspective that a person has formed, either through objective or subjective reasoning, about a topic, issue, person or thing.

introduce.o: From Middle English introducen, from Old French introduire, from Latin intrōdūcō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁énteros (“inner, what is inside”) and *dewk-.
introduce.example: Wheeled transport was introduced long ago.

reference.o: From Middle French référence, from Medieval Latin referentia, nominative neuter plural of referēns, present participle of referō (“return, reply”, literally “carry back”). Morphologically refer + -ence.
reference.example: The given pointer will reference the actual generated data.
reference.exampleSense: To contain the value that is a memory address of some value stored in memory.

cite.o:
verb: From Old French citer, from Latin citare (“to cause to move, excite, summon”), frequentative of ciēre (“to rouse, excite, call”). Sense 4 is the original one.

noun: From the first syllable of citation. Analogous to quote, from quotation.
cite.example: WikiLeaks did not cause these uprisings but it certainly informed them. The dispatches revealed details of corruption and kleptocracy that many Tunisians suspected, but could not prove, and would cite as they took to the streets.
cite.exampleSense: To quote; to repeat, as a passage from a book, or the words of another.

elicit.o: Borrowed from Latin elicitus from eliciō (“draw forth”).
elicit.example: Fred wished to elicit the time of the meeting from Jane.
elicit.exampleSense: To draw out, bring out, bring forth (something latent); to obtain information from someone or something.

quote.o: From Middle English quoten, coten (“to mark (a book) with chapter numbers or marginal references”), from Old French coter, from Medieval Latin quotāre (“to distinguish by numbers, number chapters”), itself from Latin quotus (“which, what number (in sequence)”), from quot (“how many”) and related to quis (“who”). The sense developed via “to give as a reference, to cite as an authority” to “to copy out exact words” (since 1680); the business sense “to state the price of a commodity” (1866) revives the etymological meaning. The noun, in the sense of “quotation,” is attested from 1885; see also usage note, below.
quote.example: The writer quoted the president's speech.
quote.exampleSense: To repeat (the exact words of a person).

extract.o: Borrowed from Latin extractum, neuter perfect passive participle of extrahō, from ex- (“out of”) + trahō (“to drag”).
extract.example: Please extract the cube root of 27.
extract.exampleSense: To determine (a root of a number).

abstract.o: From Middle English abstract, borrowed from Latin abstractus, perfect passive participle of abstrahō (“draw away”), formed from abs- (“away”) + trahō (“to pull, draw”). The verbal sense is first attested in 1542.
abstract.example: He abstracted out the square root function.
abstract.exampleSense: To separate; to disengage. To consider abstractly; to contemplate separately or by itself; to consider theoretically; to look at as a general quality. To produce an abstraction, usually by refactoring existing code. Generally used with "out".

summary.o:
adj: From Middle English summary, from Medieval Latin summārius, from Latin summa (“total, sum”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives).

noun: From Medieval Latin summārium, from Latin summa (“total, sum”) + -ārium (suffix forming nouns of purpose).
summary.example: A summary review is in the appendix.
summary.exampleSense: Concise, brief, or presented in a condensed form; presenting information in such a form.

assume.o: From Latin assūmō (“accept, take”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + sūmō (“take up, assume”).
assume.example: We assume that, as her parents were dentists, she knows quite a bit about dentistry.
assume.exampleSense: To authenticate by means of belief; to surmise; to suppose to be true, especially without proof

presume.o: From Middle English presumen, from Anglo-Norman presumer and its source, Latin praesūmere (“to take beforehand, anticipate”), from prae- + sūmere (“to take”).
presume.example: Thanks, but I can't accept the money; I would not want to presume on the generosity of a stranger.
presume.exampleSense: To impose (on) for one's advantage; to be presumptuous; with on, upon, to take advantage (of), to take liberties (with).

suppose.o: From Middle English supposen, borrowed from Old French supposer, equivalent to prefix sub- (“under”) + poser (“to place”); corresponding in meaning to Latin supponere (“to put under, to substitute, falsify, counterfeit”), suppositum. See pose.
suppose.example: Suppose that A implies B and B implies C. Then A implies C.

hypothesis.o: Recorded since 1596, from Middle French hypothese, from Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument, supposition”, literally “a placing under”), itself from ὑποτίθημι (hupotíthēmi, “to set before, suggest”), from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, place”). Compare hypothec.

postulate.o:
noun: Borrowed from Latin postulātum, a neuter nominalization of postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō, possibly from poscō. See -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more. Cognate with French postulat.

verb: From Latin postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō (“to request”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Cognate with French postuler.

verb: From Latin postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō (“to request”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

speculate.o: Borrowed from Latin speculātus, perfect active participle of speculor (“to watch, observe, examine, spy”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from specula (“a watchtower”), ultimately from speciō (“to look at”).
speculate.example: It is remarkable that persons who speculate the most boldly often conform with the most perfect quietude to the external regulations of society.
speculate.exampleSense: To think, meditate or reflect on a subject; to consider, to deliberate or cogitate.

predict.o: Early 17th century, from Latin praedicō (“to mention beforehand”) (perfect passive participle praedictus), from prae- (“before”) + dīcō (“to say”). Equivalent to Germanic forespeak, foretell, and foresay.
predict.example: Professor Trelawney kept predicting Harry’s death, which he found extremely annoying.
predict.exampleSense: To make a prediction: to forecast, foretell, or estimate a future event on the basis of knowledge and reasoning; to prophesy a future event on the basis of mystical knowledge or power.

perceive.o: From Middle English perceyven, borrowed from Old French percevoir, perceveir, from Latin percipiō, past participle perceptus (“take hold of, obtain, receive, observe”), from per (“by, through”) + capiō (“to take”); see capable. Compare conceive, deceive, receive.
perceive.example: Numerous experimental tests and other observations have been offered in favor of animal mind reading, and although many scientists are skeptical, others assert that humans are not the only species capable of representing what others do and don’t perceive and know.
perceive.exampleSense: To become aware of, through the physical senses, to see; to understand.

detect.o:
verb: From Latin detectus, perfect passive participle of detegere (“to uncover or disclose”), from de- + tegere (“to cover”); see tegument, tile, thatch.

verb: Back-formation from detective.
detect.example: Diesel maintenance schedules are benefiting from work done on the magnificent Hilger & Watts electronic spectrograph for oil analysis, which detects minute quantities of metals in samples of used lubricating oil; [...].
detect.exampleSense: To discover or find by careful search, examination, or probing.

discern.o: From Middle English discernen, from Old French discerner, from Latin discernere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from dis- (“apart”) + cernere (“to distinguish”); see certain.
discern.example: Meanwhile the brig had altered her tack, and was moving slowly to the east. Three hours later and the keenest eye could not have discerned her top-sails above the horizon.
discern.exampleSense: To detect with the senses, especially with the eyes.

recognize.o:
verb: Borrowed from Middle French reconoistre, from Old French reconoistre, from Latin recognoscere, first attested in the 16th century. Displaced native English acknow (“to recognize, perceive as”), compare German erkennen and Swedish erkänna. Latin had rare recognizare (“to try by jury”).

verb: From re- + cognize.
recognize.example: His services were recognized in a testimonial.
recognize.exampleSense: To show formal appreciation of, as with an award, commendation etc.

conscious.o: First use appears c. 1573 in the sense of "aware of wrongdoing".https://web.archive.org/web/20220714064352/https://www.lexico.com/definition/conscious From Latin cōnscius (“conscious, conscious of guilt”), itself from con- (a form of com- (“together”)) + scīre (“to know”) + -us.
conscious.example: Start fresh, try and learn from past mistakes, make a conscious effort to be a better person.
conscious.exampleSense: Deliberate, intentional, done with awareness of what one is doing.

reckon.o: From Middle English rekenen, from Old English recenian (“to pay; arrange, dispose, reckon”) and ġerecenian (“to explain, recount, relate”); both from Proto-West Germanic *rekanōn (“to count, explain”), from Proto-West Germanic *rekan (“swift, ready, prompt”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to make straight or right”). Cognate with Scots rekkin (“to enumerate, mention, narrate, rehearse, count, calculate, compute”), Saterland Frisian reekenje (“to calculate, figure, reckon”), West Frisian rekkenje (“to account, tally, calculate, figure”), Dutch rekenen (“to count, calculate, reckon, charge”), German Low German reken (“to reckon”), German rechnen (“to count, reckon, calculate”), Danish regne (“to calculate”), Swedish räkna (“to count, calculate, reckon”), Norwegian Nynorsk rekna (“to calculate”), Icelandic reikna (“to calculate”), Latin rectus (“straight, right”). See also reck, reach.
reckon.example: I reckoned above two hundred and fifty on the outside of the church.
reckon.exampleSense: To count; to enumerate; to number; also, to compute; to calculate.

deem.o:
verb: From Middle English dēmen (“to judge; to criticize, condemn; to impose a penalty on, sentence; to direct, order; to believe, think, deem”), from Old English dēman (“to decide, decree, deem”), from Proto-West Germanic *dōmijan, from Proto-Germanic *dōmijaną (“to judge, think”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to set, put”). The word is cognate with Danish and Norwegian Bokmål dømme (“to judge”), Dutch doemen (“to condemn, foredoom”), North Frisian dema (“to judge, recognise”), Norwegian Nynorsk døma (“to judge”), Swedish döma (“to judge, sentence, condemn”), Finnish tuomita (“to judge”). It is also related to doom.

noun: From Middle English deme, from the verb (see above).
deem.exampleSense: To hold in belief or estimation; to adjudge as a conclusion; to regard as being; to evaluate according to one's beliefs; to account.

imply.o: From Middle English implien, emplien, borrowed from Old French emplier, from Latin implicare (“to infold, involve”), from in (“in”) + plicare (“to fold”). Doublet of employ and implicate.
imply.example: The proposition that "all dogs are mammals" implies that my dog is a mammal.
imply.exampleSense: to have as a necessary consequence; to lead to (something) as a consequence

deliberate.o: Inherited from Middle English deliberat(e), borrowed from Latin dēlīberātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīberō (“to consider, weigh well”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + *līberō / lībrō (“to weigh”)), from *libera / libra (“a balance”); see librate. Doublet of deliber.
deliberate.example: It is now time for the jury to deliberate the guilt of the defendant.
deliberate.exampleSense: To consider carefully; to weigh well in the mind.

represent.o:
verb: From Old French représenter, from Latin repraesentō. Displaced native Old English spelian (“to represent”).

verb: From re- + present.
represent.example: He sent his agent to represent himself at the meeting.
represent.exampleSense: To stand or act in the place of; to perform the duties, exercise the rights, or otherwise act on behalf of

insist.o: Partly from Middle French insister, from Latin īnsistere; and partly from a back-formation from insistence. Compare typologically from the same PIE root Bulgarian настоявам (nastojavam), Russian наста́ивать (nastáivatʹ).
insist.example: Angles likewise which insist on the Diameter, are all Right Angles.
insist.exampleSense: To stand (on); to rest (upon); to lean (upon).

persist.o: From Middle French persister (Modern French persister), from Latin persistere, from per- + sistere (“to stand”).
persist.example: Throughout the period, toothy giants persisted in the oceans. Perhaps the most spectacular was the megalodon shark.

understand.o: From Middle English understanden, from Old English understandan (“to understand”), from Proto-West Germanic *understandan (“to stand between, understand”), from Proto-Germanic *understandaną (“to stand between, understand”), equivalent to Old English under- (“between, inter-”) + standan (“to stand”) (Modern English under- + stand). Cognate with Old Frisian understonda (“to understand, experience, learn”), Old High German understantan (“to understand”), Middle Danish understande (“to understand”). Compare also Saterland Frisian understunda, unnerstounde (“to dare, survey, measure”), Dutch onderstaan (“to undertake, presume”), German unterstehen (“to be subordinate”).
understand.example: Can you repeat what you just said? I didn't understand.
understand.exampleSense: (of communication or means of communication: words, statements, signs, etc.) To know the meaning of; to parse or have parsed correctly; to comprehend.

comprehend.o: From Middle English comprehenden, from Latin comprehendere (“to grasp”), from the prefix com- + prehendere (“to seize”). Doublet of comprend.
comprehend.example: In the second century of the Christian Æra, the empire of Rome comprehended the fairest part of the earth, and the most civilized portion of mankind.

analyze.o: Probably formed within English, by back-formation, or by haplology from analysis + -ize, or from Middle French analyser, from the noun analyse, from Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análusis, “a breaking up, a loosening, releasing”), from ἀναλύω (analúō, “to unloose, release, set free”), from ἀνά (aná, “on, up, above, throughout”) + λύσις (lúsis, “a loosening”), from λύω (lúō, “to unfasten”).
analyze.example: The clearest lesson is that the F.D.A. needs the power to demand adequate postmarketing studies and the resources to analyze the results.

diagnose.o: Back-formation from diagnosis. Compare also sclerose (verb).
diagnose.example: Mechanics use this extremely portable tool to diagnose engine faults, clear fault codes, and export data.
diagnose.exampleSense: To determine the cause of a problem.

infer.o: From Latin inferō, from Latin in- (“in, at, on; into”) + Latin ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”) (cognate to Old English beran, whence English bear), from Proto-Italic *ferō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti (“to bear, carry”), from the root *bʰer-. Literally “carry forward”, equivalent to “bear in”, as in concluding from a premise. Doublet of inbear.
infer.example: It is dangerous to infer too much from martial bluster in British politics: at the first hint of trouble, channelling Churchill is a default tactic for beleaguered leaders of all sorts.
infer.exampleSense: To introduce (something) as a reasoned conclusion; to conclude by reasoning or deduction, as from premises or evidence.

deduce.o: From Late Middle English deducen (“to demonstrate, prove, show; to argue, infer; to bring, lead; to turn (something) to a use; to deduct”), borrowed from Latin dēdūcere, the present active infinitive of dēdūcō (“to lead or bring out or away; to accompany, conduct, escort; (figuratively) to derive, discover, deduce”); from dē- (prefix meaning ‘from, away from’) + dūcere (the present active infinitive of dūcō (“to conduct, guide, lead; to draw, pull; to consider, regard, think”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to lead; to draw, pull”)).
deduce.example: If you leave this Isle, and got to the court of England, see what regard there will be paid to the old pedigree that deduces your descent from kings and conquerors.
deduce.exampleSense: To examine, explain, or record (something) in an orderly manner.

conclude.o: From Middle English concluden, borrowed from Latin conclūdere (“to shut up, close, end”).
conclude.example: I will conclude this part with the speech of a counsellor of state.
conclude.exampleSense: To bring to an end; to close; to finish.

analogy.o: From Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογίᾱ (analogíā), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).
analogy.example: Is there any analogy, in certain constitutions, between keeping an umbrella up, and keeping the spirits up?
analogy.exampleSense: A relationship of resemblance or equivalence between two situations, people, or objects, especially when used as a basis for explanation or extrapolation.

compare.o: From Middle English comparen, from Old French comparer, from Latin comparare (“to prepare, procure”), from compar (“like or equal to another”), from com- + par (“equal”). Displaced native Old English metan (“to compare,” also “to measure”).
compare.example: Compare the tiger's coloration with that of the zebra.
compare.exampleSense: To assess the similarities and differences between two or more things ["to compare X with Y"]. Having made the comparison of X with Y, one might have found it similar to Y or different from Y.

contrast.o: From French contraster, from Latin contrāstāre (“to resist", "to withstand”), from contrā (“against”) + stō, stāre (“to stand”).
contrast.example: Ohh, you can't fool me. This thing's top of the line! It's got two contrast knobs!
contrast.exampleSense: A difference in lightness, brightness or hue between two colours that makes them more or less distinguishable. A control on a television, etc, that adjusts the amount of contrast in the images being displayed.

overlap.o: From over- + lap. Cognate with Dutch overlap.
overlap.example: The mouse-mat overlapped the edge of the desk.
overlap.exampleSense: To extend over and partly cover something.

contradiction.o: From Middle English contradiccioun, contradiction, from Old French contradiction, from Latin contrādictiō, from contrādīcō (“speak against”).
contradiction.example: There is a contradiction in what you say: she can't be both married and single.
contradiction.exampleSense: A statement that contradicts itself, i.e., a statement that claims that the same thing is true and that it is false at the same time and in the same senses of the terms.

disagree.o: From Middle English disagre (“to refuse to assent to”), from Anglo-Norman disagreer, disagrer, desagreer (“to refuse assent”), from Old French desagreer, desagrëer (“to be disagreeable; to be unpleasant”) (modern French désagréer (“to displease”)); the English word is analysable as dis- + agree.
disagree.example: Bob says cats are friendlier than dogs, but I disagree.
disagree.exampleSense: To fail to agree; to have a different opinion or belief.

differ.o:
verb: From Middle English differren, from Old French differer, from Latin differō (“carry apart, put off, defer; differ”), from dis- (“apart”) + ferō (“carry, bear”). Compare Ancient Greek διαφέρω (diaphérō). Doublet of defer and dilate, see also infer, confer and collate, refer and relate, as well as prefer and prelate among others.

noun: From diff + -er.
differ.example: These shoes only differ from those ones in having slightly longer laces.
differ.exampleSense: Not to have the same traits or characteristics; to be unalike or distinct.

diverse.o:
adj: PIE word *dwóh₁ The adjective is derived from Middle English divers, diverse (“different, divergent”), from Anglo-Norman divers, Anglo-Norman divers, and Old French divers (“different; of various kinds”) (modern French divers), and directly from their etymon Latin dīversus (“different, diverse”), an adjective use of the perfect passive participle of dīvertō (“to divert, turn away”), from dī- (variant of dis- (prefix meaning ‘apart, in two’)) + vertō (“to turn”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to rotate; to turn”)). Doublet of divert. The adverb is derived from Middle English diverse (“differently; at various times”), from divers, diverse (adjective) (see above).

verb: From Middle English diversen (“to differ, diverge; to become different, change; to vary; to change or vary (something); to make a distinction, distinguish; to divert”), from Anglo-Norman diverser, Middle French diverser, and Old French diverser (“to alter, change; to differ, diverge; to disagree”), from Late Latin diversare (“to differ”), and then either: * a frequentative form of Latin dīvertere, the present active infinitive of dīvertō (see etymology 1); or * from dī- (variant of dis- (prefix meaning ‘apart, in two’)) + versāre (the present active infinitive of versō (“to alter, change; to keep turning, whirl”), a frequentative form of vertō: see etymology 1). Etymology 2 sense 1 (“synonym of diversify”) became obsolete in the 16th century, and was probably recoined in the 20th century.
diverse.example: 1797?, Jonathan Edwards, A Dissertation Concerning Liberty and Necessity; containing remarks on the essays of Dr. Samuel West, and on the writings of several other authors, on those subjects.
diverse.exampleSense: Different; dissimilar; distinct; not the same

nuance.o: Borrowed from French nuance (“nuance, shade, hue”). Omitting several steps, from Latin nūbēs. Compare typologically Italian sfumatura (< Latin fūmus).
nuance.example: Understanding the basics is easy, but appreciating the nuances takes years.

inductive.o: From Middle French inductif, from Late Latin inductivus.

detail.o: Borrowed from Middle French détail, from Old French detail, from detaillier, from de- + taillier (“to cut”). Compare typologically Bulgarian подробност (podrobnost), Czech podrobnost, Russian подро́бность (podróbnostʹ) (akin to дроби́ть (drobítʹ)).
detail.example: Note this fine detail in the lower left corner.
detail.exampleSense: A part small enough to escape casual notice.

thorough.o: From Middle English thoruȝ, þoruȝ, from Old English þuruh, a byform of Old English þurh, whence comes English through. The adjective derives from the preposition and adverb. The word developed a syllabic form in cases where the word was fully stressed: when it was used as an adverb, adjective, or noun, and less commonly when used as a preposition.
thorough.example: The infested house needs a thorough cleansing before it will be inhabitable.
thorough.exampleSense: Painstaking and careful not to miss or omit any detail.

example.o: From Middle English example, exaumple, from Old French example, essaumple, from Latin exemplum (“sample, pattern, specimen, copy for imitation, etc.”, literally “what is taken out”); see exempt. Doublet of exemplum and sample. Displaced native Middle English forebisne, from Old English forebȳsn; and Middle English bisne, from Old English bȳsn (modern English bizen).
example.example: If Demandt's essay served as a strident example of the German desire for normalcy, a more subtle example was provided by a brief allohistorical depiction of a Nazi victory in World War II written by German historian Michael Salewski in 1999.
example.exampleSense: Something that is representative of all such things in a group.

instance.o: Borrowed from Middle French instance, from Latin īnstantia (“a being near, presence, also perseverance, earnestness, importunity, urgency”), from īnstāns (“urgent”); see instant.
instance.example: Some compilers will allow statics to be inlined, but then incorrectly create multiple instances of the inlined variable at run-time.
instance.exampleSense: A specific occurrence of something that is created or instantiated, such as a database, or an object of a class in object-oriented programming.

confirm.o: From Middle English confirmen, confermen, from Old French confermer, from Latin cōnfirmāre (“to make firm, strengthen, establish”), from con- (“together”) + firmāre (“to make firm”), from firmus (“firm”).
confirm.example: Elizabeth, daughter of Henry VIII, was baptized and confirmed at the age of three days.
confirm.exampleSense: To administer the sacrament of confirmation on (someone).

demonstrate.o: Borrowed from Latin dēmonstrātus, the perfect passive participle of dēmonstrō (“to show, point at”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French démontrer.
demonstrate.example: Those people outside are demonstrating against the election results.
demonstrate.exampleSense: to participate in or organize a demonstration.

illustrate.example: The economics textbook was illustrated with many graphs.
illustrate.exampleSense: To provide a book or other publication with pictures, diagrams or other explanatory or decorative features.

manifest.o: From Middle English manifest, manifeste, from Latin manifestus, manufestus (“palpable, manifest”), from Latin manus (“hand”) + an uncertain second element. Doublet of manifesto.
manifest.example: And usually this manifests as them trying to prove their parent's criticism's and belittlings wrong.
manifest.exampleSense: To show plainly; to make to appear distinctly, usually to the mind; to put beyond question or doubt; to display; to exhibit.

prove.o:
verb: From Middle English proven, from Old English prōfian (“to esteem, regard as, evince, try, prove”) and Old French prover (“to prove”), both from Latin probō (“test, try, examine, approve, show to be good or fit, prove”, verb), from probus (“good, worthy, excellent”), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-bʰuH-s (“being in front, prominent”), from *pro-, *per- (“toward”) + *bʰuH- (“to be”). Displaced native Middle English sothen (“to prove”), from Old English sōþian (“to prove”). Doublet of probe. More at for, be, soothe.

verb: Simple past form of proove, conjugated as a Germanic strong verb, on the pattern of choose → chose.
prove.example: I will prove that my method is more effective than yours.
prove.exampleSense: To demonstrate that something is true or viable; to give proof for; to bear out.

determine.o: From Middle English determinen, from Old French determiner, French déterminer, from Latin determināre (“to bound, limit, prescribe, fix, determine”), from de + termināre (“to limit”), from terminus (“bound, limit, end”).
determine.example: The knowledge of men hitherto hath been determined by the view or sight.
determine.exampleSense: To set the boundaries or limits of.

decide.o: From Middle English deciden, from Old French decider, from Latin dēcīdere, infinitive of dēcīdō (“cut off, decide”), from dē (“down from”) + caedō (“cut”).
decide.example: It decides me to look into the matter, for if it is worth anyone's while to take so much trouble, there must be something in it.
decide.exampleSense: to cause someone to come to a decision

resolve.o: From Middle English resolven, from Old French resolver, a learned borrowing of Latin resolvō (“loosen, thaw, melt, resolve”), equivalent to re- + solve. Piecewise doublet of re-solve.
resolve.example: I resolve to finish this work before I go home.
resolve.exampleSense: To make a firm decision to do something. To become determined to reach a certain goal or take a certain action.

survey.o: From Middle English surveyen, from Old French sourveoir, surveer (“to oversee”), from sour-, sur- (“over”) + veoir, veeir (“to see”), from Latin videre. See sur- and vision. Related to supervision.
survey.example: He stood on a hill, and surveyed the surrounding country.
survey.exampleSense: To inspect, or take a view of; to view with attention, as from a high place; to overlook

research.o: Early Modern French rechercher (“to examine closely”), from Old French recerchier (“to seek, to look for”), by surface analysis, re- + search.
research.example: The research station that houses Wang and his team is outside Lijiang, a city of about 1.2 million people.
research.exampleSense: Diligent inquiry or examination to seek or revise facts, principles, theories, applications, etc. (that are currently available, or that are familiar to one's self).

observe.o: From Middle French observer, from Old French observer, from Latin observō (“to watch”), from ob- (“before”) + servō (“to keep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to guard”). Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐍂𐍅𐌰 (sarwa, “weapons, armour”), Old English searu (“device”).
observe.example: Please observe all posted speed limits.
